Computational overhead not quantified despite claims of being lightweight; actual FLOP/timing comparisons absent

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Compelling visualization (Fig. 2) demonstrates that pre-trained VLM representations cluster by visual appearance rather than task progress, motivating proprioceptive alignment.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Multiple benchmarks (RoboCasa-Kitchen SOTA 69.7%, LIBERO), real-world robot validation with generalization tests, extensive ablation studies, and from-scratch experiments across diverse VLM backbones.
Practical lightweight design: View cutoff augmentation adds only +1.25% computational overhead while remaining fully compatible with existing VLA training pipelines.
Strong real-world results: 13.3% absolute improvement on real-robot tasks and 41.6% improvement on close-lid task demonstrate substantial practical value beyond simulation.

Rigorous representation analysis: CKNNA and KNN classification studies (Table 5, Fig. 8) quantitatively validate that RS-CL improves task-progress structure (1.2% → 22.9%) while preserving scene information.

Thorough ablation studies: Systematic analysis of soft-label targets, augmentation strategies, hyperparameter sensitivity, and adaptation to different VLA architectures (autoregressive vs. flow-matching).
Generalization across architectures: Method successfully applies to multiple VLM backbones and proprioceptive state configurations, indicating practical robustness.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution combines existing techniques (supervised contrastive learning + proprioceptive distance weighting) in a straightforward manner without substantial methodological innovation.

Task-dependent effectiveness: Inconsistent improvements across task types—strong on pick-and-place (+11.2%) but weak/negative on open-and-close (-1.3 to +1.0%), suggesting the method conflicts with constrained action spaces and limiting generality.

Unjustified design choices: (1) Euclidean distance for proprioceptive similarity is problematic for 6D rotations which don't form Euclidean spaces; (2) specific temperature function (Eq. 4) lacks theoretical justification; (3) cosine decay schedule for λ appears arbitrary despite empirical validation.

Proprioceptive dependency and limited scope: Method requires reliable proprioceptive information during training, limiting applicability to robots with noisy/sparse feedback. Only uses end-effector pose/joint positions; doesn't incorporate contact forces, object pose, or other relevant signals that could improve results.

Modest gains on some benchmarks: LIBERO improvements of 1-2% (Table 2) and from-scratch learning with general VLMs (<5%) lack statistical significance testing and reported confidence intervals, making impact unclear.
Limited experimental scope: Real-robot evaluation restricted to single platform (Franka); 24 trials per task without error bars; no failure case analysis or guidance on when to avoid RS-CL.

Incomplete analysis: (1) Why does performance sometimes decrease on open-and-close tasks? (2) How does noisy proprioception affect performance? (3) Comparison with TCN somewhat unfair as it targets temporal consistency, not proprioceptive alignment; missing comparisons with alternative soft-weighting schemes.

Presentation issues: Paper is lengthy with important details relegated to appendix; connection between hypothesis and specific contrastive formulation could be clearer; some baseline results reproduced rather than official.
